newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania citizens committees put off disbanding.
newsitem.headline: Albania citizens committees put off disbanding.

text.p: Albania's so-called salvation committees, maverick citizens' groups set up amid rioting earlier this year, on Friday postponed a decision to disband amid worries over planned elections.

Assembling in the southern town of Vlore, at the heart of the February-March anarchy, they put off deciding whether to break up until Saturday, noting that most political parties threatened to boycott the vote.
Most participants denounced President Sali Berisha, blamed by many for the collapse of the shady pyramid investment schemes that sparked the February and March unrest.
The committees were born amid the rioting that swept Albania to protect towns from the violence and bring some order where there was none.

"We shall not disband because the situation has worsened. Under these circumstances we want to talk to political parties so the crisis can be solved with democratic means," said Latif Lato, of a committee in the southern town of Tepelene.
The groups, which Berisha has accused of being the armed wing of his Socialist arch-rivals, were to disband this week under a deal brokered by European envoy Franz Vranitzky.

Reports of the influence of the committees vary and some southern residents say they no longer have a large say. The early elections were called in March to help pacify the country and are seen as vital to restore order.
Parties threatened to boycott the vote amid fresh wrangles with Berisha's former ruling Democratic Party over the rules under which the vote will be held.
Vranitzky seemed to have secured the success of the elections on Thursday after persuading parliament once again to debate the election law but the Socialists and other parties were still unhappy.
"We do not recognise the election law this illegitimate parliament imposes on us," said Xhevat Kocia, who heads the committee of the coastal town of Sarande.
